woe

/woh/ — rhymes with know · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Woe is a deep, heavy feeling of misery, especially when troubles pile up.

The farmer's tale of woe included a flood, a drought, and a broken tractor all in one year.

Example

A small business owner describes her past year: supply chain failures left her warehouse empty, a key employee quit unexpectedly, and a data breach cost her thousands. She calls it her 'year of woe.'

The situation isn't a single sad event—it's a cascade of troubles all hitting together. 'woe' captures that compounded, stacked-up suffering, as if telling a story of disasters. Plain 'sadness' names one low moment—it doesn't convey that narrative weight.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

grief: Grief is the deep sorrow that follows a loss, usually one loss — a death, a friendship ended. Woe is wider and more theatrical: it gathers a whole run of troubles into one heavy state, the stuff of a 'tale of woe.' Grief has a single cause; woe piles its causes up.

distress: Distress is the strained, upset state of someone under pressure — worried, frightened, in need of relief. It can be brief and fixable. Woe is heavier and more sorrowful: deep misery that has settled in after trouble upon trouble. A delayed flight causes distress; a ruined year brings woe.

heartache: Heartache is emotional pain centered on love and longing — a broken friendship, a family far away. It aches quietly in one tender spot. Woe is grander and more sweeping: it covers a person's whole load of sorrow and misfortune, not just the hurt in one corner of the heart.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

joy: bright, uncomplicated happiness and delight

bliss: a state of perfect, untroubled happiness

Where it sits · how deep and sweeping the misery

sadness → sorrow → anguish → woe

sadness vs. woe: Sadness is much weaker than woe — sadness is one gloomy afternoon, while woe piles trouble upon trouble into a whole tale of misery.

sorrow vs. woe: Sorrow is deeper than plain sadness but still weaker than woe; sorrow grieves a single loss, while woe suggests a string of misfortunes weighing someone down.

anguish vs. woe: Anguish comes close to woe in intensity — anguish is one moment of searing pain — but woe is the stronger, more sweeping term, naming deep misery that colors someone's whole situation.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — wā: a cry of grief; misery, wretchedness (Old English)

Put it together: Woe began as the Old English wail of grief itself — 'wā!' — so the word literally is the cry of misery, which is why it names deep sadness and a pile-up of troubles.

Use the root in a new word: woeful: The team gave a woeful performance, so full of errors that the fans trudged home carrying a little of the players' woe themselves.

Word Building

Word Choice

formal / literary

Woe is grand and serious—the misery of kings or a tragic hero. Reach for it when troubles pile up and the suffering is deep and ongoing. For everyday unhappiness, 'sadness' is simpler and better.
